payoff.note: T > R > P > S: defecting pays more in any single round. 2R > T + S: taking turns exploiting each other pays less than steady cooperation. Defect-defect is the one-shot Nash equilibrium.

strategies.name: Tit for tat
strategies.rule: Cooperates in the first round, then copies whatever the other player did in the round before.
strategies.notebook: Higher OS, network curation: rewards cooperators, stops feeding defectors, holds no grudge once the other cooperates again.
strategies.anchor: The most common reciprocal rule people write or are estimated to play in infinitely repeated PD experiments (Dal Bo & Frechette 2019); won both of Axelrod's tournaments.
strategies.source: Rapoport's entry, Axelrod 1980a, 1980b; share: research/gametheory.json recommendedStrategyMix (judgment anchored to Thoni & Volk 2018, Fischbacher, Gachter & Fehr 2001, Kurzban & Houser 2005, Dal Bo & Frechette 2019, Fudenberg, Rand & Dreber 2012)

strategies.name: Generous tit for tat
strategies.rule: Plays tit for tat but still cooperates one time in three after the other defects (q = 1/3), so a single mistake does not start a feud.
strategies.notebook: Higher OS, forgiveness: punishes in proportion and lets a relationship recover from errors.
strategies.anchor: With noise, lab subjects favor lenient and forgiving strategies, slow to anger and fast to forgive (Fudenberg, Rand & Dreber 2012); stands in for the lenient rules the engine lacks (tit for two tats, lenient grim).
strategies.source: Nowak & Sigmund 1992 Nature 355:250; Molander 1985 JCR 29:611; share: research/gametheory.json recommendedStrategyMix (judgment anchored to Thoni & Volk 2018, Fischbacher, Gachter & Fehr 2001, Kurzban & Houser 2005, Dal Bo & Frechette 2019, Fudenberg, Rand & Dreber 2012)

strategies.name: Win-stay, lose-shift
strategies.rule: Cooperates first, repeats its last move after a good payoff (R or T) and switches after a bad one (P or S).
strategies.notebook: Higher OS, decisions by optimization: learns from its own payoff, repairs a mutual mistake in two rounds, and exploits people who never retaliate.
strategies.osNote: A judgment that departs from the research mix, which suggests 'default (reinforcement learning)': win-stay lose-shift ('Pavlov') reacts to its own last payoff without a model of the other player. It is classed 'higher' here because it decides by payoff rather than by grievance, and it repairs mutual defection. Counted as 'default', the Higher OS total would be 0.45 instead of 0.52.
strategies.anchor: Rare in lab strategy estimates (Dal Bo & Frechette 2019); a 'partner' strategy (Hilbe, Chatterjee & Nowak 2018).
strategies.caveat: With T=5, R=3, P=1, S=0 it is only neutrally stable against always defect, because R = (T+P)/2.
strategies.source: Nowak & Sigmund 1993 Nature 364:56; Kraines & Kraines 1989; share: research/gametheory.json recommendedStrategyMix (judgment anchored to Thoni & Volk 2018, Fischbacher, Gachter & Fehr 2001, Kurzban & Houser 2005, Dal Bo & Frechette 2019, Fudenberg, Rand & Dreber 2012)

strategies.name: Always cooperate
strategies.rule: Cooperates every round whatever the other player does.
strategies.notebook: Default OS, its kind face: decides by feeling (warmth, fear of isolation) instead of by evidence about the other, never curates its network, and so feeds defectors.
strategies.osNote: Classed 'default' although it is kind. The Higher OS in the notebook means deciding by optimization and meta-cognition, which includes curating one's network; unconditional cooperation uses neither. In the evolution, always-cooperate players are what let always-defect players back in.
strategies.anchor: Unconditional cooperators: none in Fischbacher, Gachter & Fehr 2001; 13% in Kurzban & Houser 2005.
strategies.source: Axelrod 1984; share: research/gametheory.json recommendedStrategyMix (judgment anchored to Thoni & Volk 2018, Fischbacher, Gachter & Fehr 2001, Kurzban & Houser 2005, Dal Bo & Frechette 2019, Fudenberg, Rand & Dreber 2012)

strategies.name: Always defect
strategies.rule: Defects every round, playing the one-round Nash equilibrium forever.
strategies.notebook: Default OS, solipsism: takes the temptation payoff whenever it is offered and ignores the future.
strategies.anchor: Free riders are 19% (Thoni & Volk 2018, 17 studies) to 30% (Fischbacher, Gachter & Fehr 2001) of subjects. Always defect is one of the three most common lab strategies, and it becomes less common as the chance of meeting again rises (Dal Bo & Frechette 2018, 2019). Everyday repeated dealings have w near 0.95, so the share is set at the low end.
strategies.source: Axelrod 1984; share: research/gametheory.json recommendedStrategyMix (judgment anchored to Thoni & Volk 2018, Fischbacher, Gachter & Fehr 2001, Kurzban & Houser 2005, Dal Bo & Frechette 2019, Fudenberg, Rand & Dreber 2012)

strategies.name: Grim trigger
strategies.rule: Cooperates until the other player defects once, then defects for the rest of the relationship.
strategies.notebook: Default OS, revenge and emotional punishment: one injury, even an accidental one, ends cooperation for good.
strategies.anchor: Grim is one of the three most common strategies in noiseless lab games (Dal Bo & Frechette 2019). With noise, people are lenient (Fudenberg, Rand & Dreber 2012), and a strict trigger feuds after the first error, so its share is set below tit for tat's. Punishing defectors activates the dorsal striatum, a reward region (de Quervain et al. 2004).
strategies.source: Friedman 1971; Axelrod 1980a (Friedman's entry, 7th); share: research/gametheory.json recommendedStrategyMix (judgment anchored to Thoni & Volk 2018, Fischbacher, Gachter & Fehr 2001, Kurzban & Houser 2005, Dal Bo & Frechette 2019, Fudenberg, Rand & Dreber 2012)

strategies.name: Random
strategies.rule: Flips a coin every round, ignoring what the other player does.
strategies.notebook: Default OS, inattention: no model of the other player at all.
strategies.anchor: Players who fit no type, or whose behavior is hump-shaped or unclassified, are 4% to 20% of subjects in strategy-method studies: Fischbacher et al. 0.14 + 0.06, Kurzban & Houser 0.04, Thoni & Volk 0.104 + 0.091. This share is what remains.
strategies.source: Axelrod 1980a (RANDOM, last); share: research/gametheory.json recommendedStrategyMix (judgment anchored to Thoni & Volk 2018, Fischbacher, Gachter & Fehr 2001, Kurzban & Houser 2005, Dal Bo & Frechette 2019, Fudenberg, Rand & Dreber 2012)

strategiesNote: populationShare is the modeled share of US adults (2025) who play each rule in everyday repeated dealings: work, neighbors, family, trade. Nobody has measured how US adults play the repeated prisoner's dilemma, so the shares are mapped from lab evidence in three steps (research recommendedStrategyMix). Step 1, the type shares from public-goods strategy-method studies (Thoni & Volk 2018, a review of 17 studies with about 7,000 subjects): conditional cooperators 0.613, free riders 0.192, hump-shaped 0.104, other 0.091. Step 2, free riders become AlwaysDefect at 0.20. Step 3, conditional cooperators (0.62) are split among the reciprocal rules using repeated-PD lab evidence. Dal Bo & Frechette 2018 and 2019 found that always defect, tit for tat and grim account for most elicited strategies, that always defect falls as the chance of meeting again rises, and that win-stay lose-shift is rare. Fudenberg, Rand & Dreber 2012 found that with noise people are lenient and forgiving. The split is TitForTat 0.25, GenerousTitForTat 0.20, Grim 0.10, WinStayLoseShift 0.07. Unconditional cooperators (0 to 0.13) give AlwaysCooperate 0.08, and the residual hump-shaped and unclassified players give Random 0.10. Two checks: the mix opens with 0.75 cooperation (0.74 after noise), inside the lab band of 0.6 to 0.8 for long, low-risk repeated games, and above one-shot play (0.47), as a mix for repeated dealings should be. Higher OS strategies total 0.52 and default OS strategies total 0.48 (0.45 and 0.55 if win-stay lose-shift is counted as default, as the research suggested; see its osNote). GamesSetup.Mix uses these shares whenever the simulated population is unavailable. EconomicLives calibrates its strategy softmax to them. If Random is left out of that softmax, renormalize the other six. Treat each share as plus or minus 0.05; the mix is a judgment, not a measurement.

shadow.meaning: Tit for tat cannot be invaded by always defect when the chance w of meeting again is at least 1/2.

collectiveStability.note: It also resists alternating defection and cooperation (Axelrod 1984, Proposition 2). This is PdPayoff.ShadowThreshold in the engine.

riskDominance.note: Above w = 0.6, grim earns more than always defect against a partner equally likely to play either: cooperation is risk dominant. Lab cooperation is reliably high only when sizeBAD is small.
riskDominance.source: Blonski, Ockenfels & Spagnolo 2011 AEJ Micro; Dal Bo & Frechette 2011 AER 101:411, 2018 JEL 56:60

wslsStability.note: Knife-edge with these payoffs, so win-stay lose-shift is fragile against always defect.

clusterInvasion.note: A cluster of tit-for-tat newcomers can invade a population of always-defect natives (each newcomer earns more than a native does) once more than 1/21 of the newcomers' dealings are with each other (Axelrod 1984, chapter 3).

noisyTitForTat.note: Two tit-for-tat players with any small noise end up earning this per round in the long run (Molander 1985).

shadow.source: Axelrod 1984 The Evolution of Cooperation, ch. 3; Axelrod & Hamilton 1981 Science 211:1390; values computed for T=5, R=3, P=1, S=0 (research/gametheory.json pdConditionsAndFormulas)

oneShotCooperation.note: Mean of 130 experiments (1958-1992). Communication raises cooperation by about 40 points. With strangers and money, the typical rate is about 0.4.
oneShotCooperation.source: Sally D. (1995) Rationality and Society 7(1):58-92; Mengel F. (2018) Economic Journal 128:3182-3209

repeatedCooperation.note: Lab columns give round-1 cooperation after subjects have played several games, from the Dal Bo & Frechette meta-analysis. When cooperation is not an equilibrium, or sizeBAD is above about 0.5, cooperation decays to below about 0.3. When w is at least 0.75 and sizeBAD is low, it rises to 0.6-0.8 or more. Nulls mean the survey gives no band. The w = 0 row is the one-shot benchmark. Model columns are exact values for the modeled US mix at noise 0.02: the share of all moves that cooperate, and points per round. The mix opens with 0.74 cooperation at every w, which sits inside the lab band for long games. Its mean over all moves falls as w rises, because longer games give reciprocators time to punish defectors and to feud after mistakes. In the lab, cooperation rises with w because people switch strategies (fewer always defect). A fixed mix cannot do that; let the mix depend on w if that response is needed.
repeatedCooperation.source: Dal Bo & Frechette 2011 AER 101:411-429, 2018 JEL 56:60-114 (pattern; exact rates by treatment not reproduced in the research); model: computed from the engine's rules
repeatedCooperation.confidence: medium for the pattern, low for the band edges

withPunishment.note: Approximate share of endowment by period 10 with peer punishment (Fehr & Gachter 2000: groups of 4, MPCR 0.4, 20 tokens).

cities.note: Mean contribution with punishment, from 5.7 (Athens) to about 18 (Boston) of 20 tokens across 16 cities. Antisocial punishment of cooperators is common where civic norms are weak.

punishmentPays.note: Punishment lowers net earnings over 10 periods and raises them over 50.

publicGoods.source: Ledyard 1995 Handbook of Experimental Economics; Chaudhuri 2011 Exp Econ 14:47-83; Zelmer 2003 Exp Econ 6:299; Fehr & Gachter 2000 AER 90:980, 2002 Nature 415:137; Herrmann, Thoni & Gachter 2008 Science 319:1362; Gachter, Renner & Sefton 2008 Science 322:1510
publicGoods.confidence: high for the decay, medium for the levels

trustGame.note: 'sent' is the share of the endowment sent. 'returned' is the share of the tripled amount sent back.
trustGame.source: Johnson N.D. & Mislin A.A. (2011) J. Econ. Psych. 32:865-889; Berg, Dickhaut & McCabe 1995 GEB 10:122-142

smallScaleSocieties.note: Mean offers range from the Machiguenga (0.26) to the Lamalera (0.58) and rise with market integration.

ultimatum.note: Rejecting a low offer costs the responder money in order to punish: emotional punishment in the notebook's terms. Unfair offers activate the anterior insula (Sanfey et al. 2003).
ultimatum.source: Oosterbeek, Sloof & van de Kuilen 2004 Exp Econ 7:171-188; Camerer 2003; Henrich et al. 2005 BBS 28:795

discontinuity.note: Groups dealing with groups choose the competitive option far more often than individuals dealing with individuals. The lab gap is roughly 20-40 points of competitive choices. The mechanisms are fear (a distrustful schema of the out-group) and greed (shared responsibility, and in-group support for self-interest). The effect is larger with face-to-face talk between groups and when groups must reach consensus, and smaller when the payoffs are not a pure PD. Model: the tribe game at the spec settings is 0.2646 less cooperative than person-vs-person play of the same mix, inside the lab band.
discontinuity.source: Wildschut, Pinter, Vevea, Insko & Schopler 2003 Psych Bull 129(5):698-722; Insko et al. 1990 JPSP 58:68; Schopler & Insko 1992 Eur Rev Soc Psych 3:121
discontinuity.confidence: low-medium for d (recalled), medium for the direction

ingroupFavoritism.note: People cooperate more with in-group members, more so when group membership is common knowledge. openingDrop is d times the SD of a cooperate-or-not choice at the mix's opening cooperation of 0.74: 0.32 x sqrt(0.74 x 0.26) = 0.14. It sets spec.distrust. People help their own group far more than they hurt the other (Halevy, Bornstein & Sagiv 2008). Third parties punish violations against in-group victims more (Bernhard, Fischbacher & Fehr 2006). Parochialism and altruism thrive together when groups fight (Choi & Bowles 2007).
ingroupFavoritism.source: Balliet, Wu & De Dreu 2014 Psych Bull 140:1556-1581

rows: Thoni & Volk 2018 Econ Letters 171:37-40 (review of 17 studies)

labStrategies.dalBoFrechette2019: When subjects design strategies to play in their place, always defect, tit for tat and grim account for most choices. Always defect falls as the chance of meeting again rises, and win-stay lose-shift is rare (AER 109:3929-3952).

fudenbergRandDreber2012.finding: With 1/8 execution noise, people use lenient and forgiving strategies: slow to anger, fast to forgive. Tit-for-tat-like retaliation persists (AER 102:720-749).

labStrategies.hilbeChatterjeeNowak2018: Partners (nice, never letting a co-player gain more than R without getting R themselves) versus rivals (never outscored). Lab subjects mostly play partner strategies when those are stable (Nature Human Behaviour 2:469-477).

conformity.note: In Asch's line-judgment studies, people conformed on about a third of critical trials, and conformity has declined since (Bond & Smith 1996). This anchors spec.alphaSway.
conformity.source: Asch 1956; Bond & Smith 1996 Psych Bull 119:111 (via research/psychology.json)

tribes.partyIdNote: Shares of US adults in each tribe, summing to 1 each year. dem = strong and weak Democrats, rep = strong and weak Republicans, ind = independents including leaners, plus other parties and the apolitical: everyone outside the two tribes. This is Gallup's three-way split; the GSS 2024 values (D 25.3, I 45.5 + 2.5 other, R 26.6) match Gallup 2024 (28/43/28) within a few points. 1952-1968: ANES, recalled (ANES Guide to Public Opinion, Table 2A.1, +-2 points). 1972-2024: GSS microdata, every survey year, never more than 4 years apart. 2025: GSS 2024 shifted by Gallup's 2024 to 2025 change (D -1, I +2, R -1; Gallup Jan 2026: record 45% independents). Gallup's levels, rescaled to sum to 1, are in partyIdGallup; they were not spliced in because the two series differ by 2-5 points on independents. These are cross-sections of all adults, not of 18-year-olds. A model that fixes each person's party at the value for the year they turned 18 will make older cohorts too Democratic (D 0.52 in 1964 against 0.25 in 2024). Calibrate so that each year's adult shares match these rows instead. GamesSetup.Tribe maps tribe 0 to dem (tribe A) and tribe 1 to rep (tribe B).
tribes.partyIdGallupNote: Gallup annual averages ('Republican, Democrat or independent?'), rescaled to sum to 1. Gallup's published shares leave out other parties and no answer, so they sum to 97-100: 2025 is D 27, I 45, R 27 as published (0.273/0.454/0.273 here), 2023 is 27/43/27. 2025 is verified-secondary (Gallup Jan 2026; with leaners D 47, R 42), as are the independent shares of 2014, 2023 and 2024. 1988, 2008 and 2021 are recalled with low to medium confidence.
tribes.partyIdWithLeanersNote: GSS with leaners counted as partisans: ind = pure independents plus other parties. Leaners vote and feel like partisans, so this split suits a two-tribe picture with a small neutral middle.
tribes.trustNote: GSS TRUST: share saying 'most people can be trusted', against 'can't be too careful' or 'depends'. Every year the item was asked, 1972-2024: it was not asked in 1974, 1977, 1982 or 1985, nor in comparable form in 2021. The series is held flat before 1972. The GSS moved to mixed web and face-to-face interviews in 2021-2024, which may explain part of the 2018-2022 drop. Trust can set the chance of cooperating first with a stranger. It is strongly age-graded today (trustByAge), and the decline is mostly generational replacement (trustByBirthDecade).
tribes.ideologicalSortingNote: Weighted correlation of GSS party identification (0-6) with ideology (1-7). It rose from 0.17 (1974) to 0.63 (2024): each tribe has become ideologically uniform. In 2024, 62% of Democrats call themselves liberal (33% in 1974) and 75% of Republicans call themselves conservative (44% in 1974).
tribes.trustGovernmentNote: Trust the federal government to do what is right 'just about always' or 'most of the time' (ANES via Pew; Pew 2023, 2024).

affectivePolarization.thermometerNote: Partisans' mean rating of the other party on the ANES 0-100 feeling thermometer: about 45-48 in the late 1970s and 1980s (46.5 is the midpoint), about 30 by 2016, about 20 by 2020. In-party ratings held at about 70-75 (72.5). The gap is in-party minus out-party. distrustIndex is the gap divided by its 2020 value, held at 1 after 2020. It is derived and optional: multiply spec.distrust by it for a distrust that changes over time. The US rose fastest among 12 OECD countries (Boxell, Gentzkow & Shapiro 2024).
affectivePolarization.source: ANES via Iyengar, Lelkes, Levendusky, Malhotra & Westwood 2019 Annu Rev Polit Sci 22:129; Pew Research Center 2016, Aug 2022; Almond & Verba 1960 and YouGov 2010 via Iyengar, Sood & Lelkes 2012 POQ 76:405; Boxell, Gentzkow & Shapiro 2024 REStat 106:557
affectivePolarization.confidence: medium for Pew and the marriage item, low-medium for the thermometer values (approximate)

crossPartyMarriage.note: About 4% of married couples are a Democrat married to a Republican. If spouses paired at random by party, 2 x D x R = 0.136 of couples would be Democrat-Republican (GSS 2018/2022 mean shares D 0.284, R 0.24, strong and weak partisans only), so cross-party marriages run at about 0.29 of chance. About 30% of couples in voter files are mixed once an unaffiliated or independent spouse counts. Spousal agreement on party now rivals agreement on religion (Iyengar, Konitzer & Tedin 2018).
crossPartyMarriage.source: Wang W. (Nov 2020) Institute for Family Studies; Hersh E. & Ghitza Y. (2018) PLoS ONE 13(10):e0203997; randomExpectation derived from GSS party shares

discontinuity.source: Wildschut et al. 2003 Psych Bull 129:698 (recalled, low-medium confidence)

tribes.note: The two tribes of the games station are the two parties: Democrats against Republicans, with independents outside both. Since 1972, partisans have become fewer but more alike. Strong partisans were 26% of adults in 1972 and 30% in 2024, after troughs near 20% around 1980 and in 1998; they are now well over half of all partisans (39% in 1972). Independents, leaners included, rose from 29% of adults in 1972 to 46% in 2024 (GSS); Gallup's 45% in 2025 is its record. Party and ideology have fused (correlation 0.17 in 1974, 0.63 in 2024). Feelings toward the other side have soured: the out-party thermometer fell from about 46 (late 1970s) to about 20 (2020), and Republicans upset at a child marrying a Democrat rose from 5% (1960) to 49% (2010). Trust in strangers fell from 0.47 (1972) to 0.25 (2024). The other side is now an out-group in the sense of the lab literature, hence spec.distrust.

relationships.married25to54Note: GSS, share of adults 25-54 currently married (Pew/ACS: 0.67 in 1990, 0.53 in 2019).

closeFriends.source: Gallup 1990; Survey Center on American Life, American Perspectives Survey May 2021

relationships.eveningWithFriendsNote: GSS: spends a social evening with friends several times a month or more.

lonelyDaily.note: Felt loneliness 'a lot of the day yesterday' (Gallup Panel Oct 2024); men 15-34, Gallup World Poll 2025.

dunbar.note: Number of stable relationships; contested (Lindenfors et al. 2021: 95% CI about 4-520).

relationships.note: Repeated games need repeated partners. Spouses, close friends and regular evenings with friends have all thinned since 1990, so more of a person's dealings are short, low-w games where the lab says cooperation unravels. EconomicLives can use married25to54 for the spouse partner. The continuation knob shows the same effect on the station.
relationships.source: research/behavior.json (relationshipsLonelinessFriends, gssMarriageChildlessness, gssSocialEvenings, socialTimeTrend_ATUS; Kannan & Veazie 2023 SSM Popul Health)

specNotes.noise: Chance that a move comes out the other way, per player per round. Axelrod's noisy rerun used 0.01 (Wu & Axelrod 1995); the lab's designed noise was 0.125 (Fudenberg, Rand & Dreber 2012). 0.02 doubles the classic value to stand for everyday misreadings. In a 20-round game, 1 - 0.98^40 = 55% of games then contain at least one mistake, enough to show tit for tat's feuds and grim's lockouts.
specNotes.continuation: Chance w of meeting again after each round, giving a mean of 1/(1-w) = 20 rounds. This sits above the shadow-of-the-future threshold 2/3, and sizeBAD is 0.027, so cooperation is risk-dominant. It stands for coworkers and neighbors (research simulationSpec: 0.95 for people, 0.99 for tribes or states).
specNotes.tribeSize: Members per tribe on the station. Forager bands have 25-30 members; Choi & Bowles 2007 simulated groups of about 26. 24 also keeps the pyramid legible. GamesLayer clamps it to 6-120.
specNotes.distrust: Extra chance that a member's cooperative move toward the other tribe turns into a defection (always cooperate is exempt). Derivation: in-group favoritism d = 0.32 (Balliet, Wu & De Dreu 2014), times the SD of a cooperate-or-not choice at the mix's opening cooperation of 0.74, gives an opening drop of 0.32 x sqrt(0.74 x 0.26) = 0.140. Divided by the share of opening moves the penalty can hit (0.67 x (1 - 2 x 0.02) = 0.643), that is 0.218, rounded to 0.22. Check against the discontinuity literature: the tribe game at these settings (2,000 simulated 30-round games, Python port of TribeGame) cooperates on 0.2772 of moves, against 0.542 for person-vs-person play of the same mix. The gap is 0.2646: inside the lab's 0.20-0.40, and below the d = 0.79 conversion (0.79 x 0.5 = 0.40), as expected when members decide one by one rather than by group consensus. Of that gap, tribal memory accounts for 0.1225, alpha sway for 0.05 and distrust for 0.092. The code's fallback of 0.08 would give a gap of 0.209.
specNotes.alphaSway: Extra chance that members defect after their own alpha defected toward the other tribe. Anchor: in Asch's studies people conformed on about 1/3 of critical trials, and conformity has declined since (Bond & Smith 1996). 0.25 represents a present-day follower and equals the code's default. Low confidence: no study measures leader-led defection between parties. In the tribe game it lowers cooperation by about 0.05.
specNotes.mutation: Share of each generation reseeded evenly across the six evolving strategies, so none dies out (cultural turnover). At 0.01 the 200-generation stream shows always defect collapsing within about 10 generations, then generous tit for tat and win-stay lose-shift rising. The research's default of 0.001 gives the same arc with lower floors.
specNotes.generations: Length of the replicator stream. Documentation only: GamesLayer uses its constant Generations = 200.
specNotes.gamesPerPair: Games per pair of strategies when estimating the payoff matrix. Documentation only: GamesLayer uses its constant GamesPerPair = 200. At 200 games, the engine's matrix (seed 7307) is off the exact one by 0.023 per cell on average, and by 0.125 at worst.
specNotes.partyInheritance: Chance a person takes a parent's party, the value in DESIGN.md's EconomicLives contract (its earlier overview says 0.7). It is not in the research files. Low-confidence support from recall: Jennings & Niemi 1968 APSR 62:169 found a parent-child party correlation of about 0.47 among 1965 high-school seniors. Treat it as a knob.

checks.matrixNote: Row strategy against column strategy, in PdStrategy order. 'cooperation' is the share of the row player's moves that cooperate; 'payoff' is points per round for the row player. Both are exact ratios of expectations over game lengths drawn with continuation w, which is what PrisonersDilemma.PayoffMatrix estimates; its 400-round cap barely matters at w = 0.95. The engine with 4,000 games per pair matches within 0.033 in every cell. With the station's 200 games per pair (seed 7307), the mean error is 0.023 and the worst cell is off by 0.125. EconomicLives can use 'cooperation' as its coop[mine, theirs] table.
checks.fitnessNote: Points per round each strategy earns against the US mix. Reciprocators (tit for tat 2.33, grim 2.31) out-earn always defect (2.07), but everyone falls well short of R = 3. payoffShortfall is R - mixPayoff in points per round (not a cooperation share): the mix loses 0.78 points per round (26% of R) to defectors (always defect, random), retaliation and mistakes. spec.distrust plays no part here; it applies only between tribes.

replicator.note: Exact payoff matrix and Replicator.Step, starting from the mix restricted to the six evolving strategies. engineRows come from the engine itself (PayoffMatrix with 200 games per pair, seed 7307, then Replicator), as the station runs it when the shares come from this file. Its Monte Carlo matrix moves shares by up to about 0.05 by generation 200.

tribeGame.note: Python port of TribeGame. Tribes of 24 are apportioned from the mix as in GamesSetup.Apportion; each game is 30 rounds at noise 0.02, averaged over 2,000 games (+-0.005). personBaseline is the exact cooperation of random pairs from the same mix over 30 rounds.

checks.basis: computed 2026-10-01 (scratchpad games_build/analyze.py, calib2.py); the T=5,R=3,P=1,S=0 matrices at w=0.95, eps=0.01 reproduce research/gametheory.json payoffMatrix_w0p95_eps0p01 exactly

thesis: The thesis under test: 'a lot of people buy fantasy and very few actually follow a life path that they control.' On how people treat each other, the games evidence does not support 'very few'. About half of lab subjects play reciprocal, rule-based strategies (modeled Higher OS share 0.52), and reciprocators out-earn defectors against today's mix. What has eroded is the environment those strategies need: a long shadow of the future, and trust. Trust in strangers fell from 0.47 (1972) to 0.25 (2024), and to 0.11 among 18-29s. Marriages and close friendships thinned, and the other party became an out-group. In the model, a reasoner among defectors and mistakes earns 2.3 of a possible 3 points per round. Control over one's dealings is limited by the setting, not only by the self.
